Day 77 of 100 · Kubernetes

Kubernetes ConfigMaps

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityKubernetesPublished artifact recovered

ConfigMaps separate non-sensitive application configuration from container images and can deliver values as environment variables or projected files.

Architecture / mental model

ConfigMap → env/envFrom OR projected volume → Pod/application

How it works

Configuration such as environment names, URLs and logging levels can live in a ConfigMap instead of being baked into an image. The Pod then references the ConfigMap at runtime.

Environment-variable consumption is fixed for the lifetime of the running process. Updating the ConfigMap does not rewrite environment variables inside an existing container, so the workload must be restarted or replaced to consume new values.

Normal projected ConfigMap volume files can update eventually. Files mounted with `subPath` do not receive those automatic updates, which is the field detail that turns many apparently-correct configuration changes into stale containers.

Hands-on reference

kubectl create configmap web-config --from-literal=APP_ENV=development --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info -n dev
kubectl get configmap web-config -n dev
kubectl describe configmap web-config -n dev

Verification

Consume the same key once as an environment variable and once through a normal ConfigMap volume in a lab, update the ConfigMap and observe the different behavior. Repeat with `subPath` to prove it stays stale.

Field note / gotcha

ConfigMap `subPath` mounts do not receive automatic updates. Normal projected volumes can update eventually; environment variables require a restart/replacement to change.

Security considerations

ConfigMaps are for non-confidential values. Do not put passwords, tokens or private keys there merely because the object lives inside Kubernetes.

What I learned

Externalizing configuration only helps when you understand how and when the application actually receives updates.
